Query planning against real data volume and latency needs is the level below this worth digging into once you know row counts and QPS.

At 38K rows on a single Postgres instance, this doesn't need a separate search service — Postgres full-text search fits, in the same database and pool `db.js` already uses.

Add a generated `tsvector` column to `products` (weighted: `name` higher than `description`) with a GIN index, then query it with `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word input the way users type it) ranked by `ts_rank`, as a new `GET /search?q=` route alongside the existing `products.js` handlers.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Typo/partial-word tolerance** — plain FTS only matches whole lexemes. If "wireles" or mid-word substrings need to match, add `pg_trgm` with a GIN trigram index and blend it in; skip it if exact-word search is good enough for launch.
- **Result ranking beyond text match** — plain `ts_rank` ignores business signals like `active`/popularity. Decide now if search should also weight those, since it changes the query shape.

Left for the next level down: pagination/limit shape for search results, and whether `active = false` products should ever surface.

Recommended approach: client-side downscale/compress before upload, then direct-to-object-storage (S3/GCS) via presigned URLs rather than routing image bytes through your app server — for phone camera photos (often 3–12MB, 4000x3000+), that's the difference between a fast upload and a slow, server-CPU-heavy one.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Where resizing happens.** Client-side (browser/`canvas` or mobile SDK) resize to something like max 2000px before upload is simplest and cheapest, but you lose the original. If you want to preserve originals (e.g., for future high-res needs), upload full-size to storage and generate display/thumbnail sizes async via a Lambda/Cloud Function triggered on upload — more infra, better fidelity.
2. **Sync vs async attachment to the listing.** Uploading during listing creation (upload completes, then listing references it) is simple but leaves orphaned files when a seller abandons the flow. A pending-upload record with a TTL cleanup job (or attach-on-publish) avoids storage bloat but adds a bit of state to manage.

Also worth building in given the phone-camera source: strip EXIF (photos often carry GPS coordinates of the seller's location — real privacy/safety issue), and resumable/chunked upload so a photo doesn't fail outright on a spotty cellular connection.

Direct-to-S3 signed PUT, not through the app server. Client asks the API for a signed PUT URL, uploads the photo bytes straight to S3 with it, then calls back to register the key.

This is forced, not just preferred: `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, and per `nginx.conf:5-9` that limit is pinned by the payments team's PCI paperwork — no raise, no per-location override. A phone camera photo is routinely several MB, so any upload routed through the app (`proxy_pass` to storefront) would be rejected by nginx before your code ever saw it.

Most of the plumbing already exists:
- `storage.js:14-17` already supports `method: 'PUT'` in `signedUrl`, and the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com` (comment says it was set up for exactly this, unused so far).
- `db.js:10-12` already has `addPhotoKey` to append a key to `listings.photo_keys`.

What's missing is two endpoints in `routes/listings.js`: one that generates a key server-side and returns `storage.signedUrl(key, {method:'PUT'})` (generate the key server-side, don't trust a client-supplied one — otherwise a seller can overwrite another listing's photo by guessing/reusing its key), and one the client calls after the S3 PUT succeeds to run `db.addPhotoKey`, since S3 can't call back into Postgres itself.

Left out of this shape: resizing/thumbnails, content-type/size enforcement on the S3 side (bucket policy conditions on the presigned POST/PUT), and malware scanning — next-level concerns once the basic path works.

Cache-aside in Redis, keyed by product ID, storing the assembled page data (not raw query rows) so a hit skips the DB entirely. Invalidate explicitly on writes to that product (and dependent data like price/inventory) rather than relying on TTL alone, with a short TTL (minutes) as a backstop for missed invalidations.

Two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Invalidation trigger**: event-driven (write path publishes a "product changed" event, cache worker evicts the key) versus TTL-only. Event-driven keeps pages fresh after price/stock changes; TTL-only is simpler but serves stale data for up to the TTL window.
- **Cache layer**: app-level cache (Redis) versus edge/CDN full-page cache. If pages are the same for all visitors (no per-user pricing/personalization), CDN caching removes the request from your servers entirely and beats Redis on latency; if pages vary per user, Redis is the only option and the CDN can't help.

Which one fits depends on whether these pages differ per visitor — that's the detail worth nailing down before picking.

The DB isn't really the bottleneck to build around — the CDN already sits in front of every request (CDN.md) and will cache anything the app tells it to. It doesn't, because `security` middleware (`app.js:9`, `middleware/security.js:8`) sets `no-store, no-cache, private` on *every* route, including `/p`. That was an overbroad fix for an account-page cache leak (`routes/account.js`) — the product route's own comment says nothing on the page varies by user, so it never needed that policy.

Two things actually fork the design:

1. **Scope the no-store off `/p`.** Mount `security` only on the account router, or have `routes/products.js` set its own `Cache-Control` (e.g. `public, max-age=300`) after the shared middleware runs. Product + related data changes "a few times a day" per `db.js:4`, so a few minutes of edge staleness is fine, and this alone lets the CDN start serving the 600ms `relatedProducts` join and the 40ms lookup for free — no new infrastructure, no invalidation plumbing.

2. **Stock doesn't fit that TTL.** It's shared across users (safe to cache), but changes with every order, so baking it into a 5-minute page cache shows stale quantities. Either accept that staleness, or pull `stockFor` out of the cached HTML and serve it from its own short-TTL (5–30s) cache — in-process or Redis — fetched separately, so the slow/rarely-changing part of the page gets the long CDN TTL and the fast-changing part gets a cheap short-lived cache instead of hitting Postgres per view.

Start with (1) — a one-line header scoping fix that recovers most of the ~900ms without touching infrastructure — then decide on stock once you know whether exact quantity matters on the page.

Key by `client_id`, not IP — the middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves that from `X-Api-Key` before any handler runs, and NAT sharing plus multi-address clients make IP keying wrong anyway. Enforce it in that same middleware, right after `req.client` is set, using the existing Redis client from `redis.js` — it's already the only state shared across the 4 workers and across boxes, same reason it holds sessions.

For the counter itself: a Lua script doing `INCR` + conditional `PEXPIRE` on `ratelimit:{client_id}:{window}` is the one real fork against a token bucket. Fixed/sliding-window INCR is simpler and atomic in one round trip; token bucket tolerates bursts better but needs a Lua script tracking last-refill time per key. Given one client is *steadily* hammering the endpoint rather than bursting, window-counter is the simpler fix here.

On limit exceeded: `429` with `Retry-After`, short-circuit before the `db.query` calls so Postgres never sees the excess load — that's the actual thing protecting other clients.

Left out: per-plan limits (the `plan` column is already fetched, so tiering is a later parameter change, not a redesign), and whether the limit is per-route or per-account across all of `/v1`.

Recommendation: token-bucket limiter keyed per client (API key or auth token, not IP — IP is unreliable behind shared NAT/proxies and easy to spoof), returning 429 with a `Retry-After` header once a client exceeds its bucket. That isolates the noisy client without touching everyone else's traffic.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Where it's enforced** — at a gateway/proxy in front of the service (nginx, Envoy, or an API gateway) if you have one, versus middleware inside the app. Gateway-level is cheaper (rejects before your app does any work) but only works if all `/v1` traffic already passes through one.
2. **Where the counters live** — in-memory per instance is fine only if `/v1` runs as a single instance; if it's horizontally scaled, counters need to be centralized (Redis, e.g. via GCRA/leaky-bucket script) or the limit becomes per-instance and the client just gets N× the intended budget by hitting different instances.

What's `/v1` running on — a single instance behind a gateway, or scaled out? That determines which of the two you need.

Polling, not push — the platform rules out anything else. `PLATFORM.md` blocks WebSocket upgrades (501 at the edge) and kills any invocation at 10s, so an SSE stream would die immediately too; there's also no sticky routing or shared memory to hold a connection across instances even if timeouts allowed it.

So: replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with `setInterval(load, …)`, keep hitting the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint (already cheap: 4KB, 30ms), and skip re-rendering when the returned `computed_at` matches what's already on screen.

The one real decision is the interval. `rollup` only changes once a minute on a fixed schedule (`jobs/rollup.md`), so anything faster than that buys nothing — 15–20s keeps the UI within a few seconds of a rollup while it stays well clear of the 60s cadence. Tighter tuning (visibility-based backoff when the tab isn't focused, retry/backoff on fetch failure) is the part I'd leave for implementation, not upfront design.

Poll — the platform rules out push. `api/` functions get frozen between invocations (db.js:1-11) and WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge (PLATFORM.md:9-10), so nothing can hold a connection open or notify a client on its own; that's not a design choice, it's fixed by PLATFORM.md.

Given that, the fork that matters is polling interval vs. the actual data cadence: `rollup` only changes once a minute (jobs/rollup.md:3), so polling faster than that just burns function invocations for identical rows. In `public/dashboard.js`, replace the click-only `load()` with a `setInterval` around 20-30s, and skip the re-render when `computed_at` (already returned by `api/metrics.js:8`) hasn't changed since the last poll. Drop the refresh button once this lands.

Left out: backoff/retry on a failed poll, and what happens if the rollup job itself runs late — neither is a UI decision.

Two decisions actually fork this design, given `PROVIDER.md`'s idempotency guarantee and the fact that a timeout means *unknown*, not *failed*:

**1. Idempotency key, keyed by order.** Every attempt for a given order must send the same `Idempotency-Key` (e.g. derived from `order.id`), including retries. Without that, retrying a request that actually succeeded but timed out on the response leg double-charges the customer — the vendor's dedup guarantee only helps if you use it.

**2. Retry only the failure classes that are actually retriable, and stop calling it "failed" when you give up.** In `payments.charge()`, retry on timeout and network error and 5xx (with backoff and a small bounded attempt count, since the 10s timeout already eats most of the request budget), but never on 4xx — a decline is a real, final answer. When retries are exhausted, `routes/checkout.js:31` shouldn't say "payment failed": the true state is still unknown, so the order should land in a `needs_reconciliation`/pending state and get resolved out-of-band (a job that replays the same idempotency key against the vendor, or a webhook) rather than lying to the customer that it failed.

Skipped: exact backoff schedule/attempt count, and the reconciliation job's mechanics.

Two things make this safe to build, both visible in the files:

- **Idempotency-Key is the load-bearing piece.** `payments.js` never sends one (PROVIDER.md:20), and `PROVIDER.md:7-11` says a timeout must be treated as *unknown*, not failed — the charge may have gone through. Retrying without that header risks a real double-charge. Generate a stable key once per order (e.g. `order.id` or a UUID persisted before the first attempt) and send it on every attempt for that order, retry included.
- **Don't retry synchronously inside the request handler.** `checkout.js:20-30` awaits `payments.charge` directly and maps any throw to `502 payment failed` — stacking retries there just makes the customer wait 20-30s and still risks a false "failed" if all attempts time out. Instead: on timeout, write the order as `payment_processing` (not `failed`) with the idempotency key stored, return that status to the client, and retry with the same key out of band (background job or next webhook/poll) until you get a definitive result — success or a genuine decline — then flip status to `paid`/`failed`.

That's the fork: synchronous bounded retry (simpler, but customer still stares at a spinner and can still see a wrong "failed" if retries exhaust) vs. async reconciliation with a `payment_processing` state (correct given the vendor's "unknown means unknown" guidance, more moving parts — needs a poller or webhook and a UI state for "processing").

Two forks decide this:

**Where the index lives.** If products already live in a relational DB (Postgres), start there: a `tsvector` column combining name + description, GIN-indexed, ranked with `ts_rank`. Add `pg_trgm` for typo-tolerant/substring matches on product names. No new infra, good enough for tens of thousands of products. Move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch, Typesense, or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) once you need sub-50ms latency at scale, faceted filtering, or better relevance tuning than Postgres offers — that's a real migration, not a tweak, so worth deciding now if you know volume/latency targets.

**How matching works.** Plain keyword/prefix matching is cheap and ships fast but misses typos and synonyms ("sneaker" vs "shoe"). Fuzzy/typo-tolerant matching (trigram or the built-in fuzzy search in Typesense/Meilisearch) covers real user queries much better and is what most "search bar" UX expects.

Recommendation: Postgres `tsvector` + `pg_trgm` if you're already on Postgres and volume is moderate — it's a day of work, not a new service. Indexing pipeline, ranking/weighting (name > description), and pagination are the depth I'm skipping — what's the current DB and rough product count?

Two forking decisions:

1. **Where matching happens.** If products already live in a relational DB and volume is modest (up to ~a few hundred thousand rows), Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` + GIN index, or `pg_trgm` for fuzzy/typo tolerance) covers this with no new infrastructure. If you want typo-tolerance, relevance ranking, and search-as-you-type out of the box, a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense) is worth the extra service — it's noticeably better UX for less tuning work than rolling your own ranking in SQL.
2. **How the index stays fresh.** Sync the search index on product create/update (via app-layer write-through or a DB trigger/CDC pipeline) rather than batch-reindexing, so new products are searchable immediately.

My pick: start with Postgres full-text search if you're already on Postgres — it's the lowest-risk path and can be swapped for Meilisearch/Typesense later without changing the product API if search volume or relevance demands grow.

Left out: ranking/synonym tuning, filtering/facets, and semantic (embedding-based) search for paraphrase matching — worth a follow-up pass once basic keyword search ships.

Client-side compress/resize before upload, then send straight to object storage via a presigned URL — the app server only stores the resulting metadata row (listing_id, key, position), not the bytes.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **Resize on the client vs. upload the raw phone photo.** Phone cameras produce 3–10MB HEIC/JPEG files; resizing to something like 2000px longest edge via canvas/`createImageBitmap` before upload cuts upload time and mobile data use dramatically, at the cost of a bit of client complexity (and HEIC decoding support varies by browser). Worth it for a seller on cellular.
- **Direct-to-storage (presigned PUT) vs. proxying through your app server.** Presigned URLs keep large uploads off your server's request/memory budget and scale better; proxying is simpler to reason about (one auth path, no CORS/presign plumbing) but chokes your server on big multi-photo batches. Direct-to-storage is the better default here.

Left out: generating thumbnails/derived sizes (async worker on an upload-complete event, not inline), EXIF orientation/stripping GPS data, retry/resume for flaky mobile connections, and photo ordering/reordering UI — each is a next-level detail once the two forks above are settled.

Direct-to-S3 presigned PUT, extending what's already half-built in `storage.js:10-13` — the bucket already accepts signed PUT with the same credentials and CORS already allows it from `market.example.com`. That's not incidental: `nginx.conf:11-13` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, and the comment there says raising it (even per-location) was already requested and declined for PCI reasons. A phone photo is routinely 3-8MB, so routing upload bytes through the storefront service would 413 at the proxy — the only path that isn't blocked is the client uploading straight to S3, past nginx entirely.

Shape: an endpoint returns a presigned PUT URL for a generated key (`listings/{id}/{uuid}.jpg`), the client PUTs the file bytes directly to S3, then a small follow-up call with just the key hits `db.addPhotoKey` (`db.js:10-12`) to append it to `listings.photo_keys`, which is already a `text[]` waiting for exactly this. Reading photos back reuses the existing pattern in `routes/listings.js:14-17` — signed GET per key.

Two things actually fork the design:
- **Upload confirmation**: since S3 never tells the app a PUT landed, something has to call back after the browser's upload resolves. A client-side confirm call matches the existing code shape but is lost if the tab closes mid-upload; an S3 event notification is more reliable but is new infra.
- **Constraining what lands in the bucket**: once the client talks to S3 directly, nothing server-side inspects the bytes. The presigned URL can be signed with a `Content-Type`/size condition to keep it to images of sane size — worth deciding now since it's a signature-time choice, not something bolted on later.

Thumbnailing/resizing for listing thumbnails is the next layer down, not needed to get upload working.

Cache the read path, not the render, unless every visitor sees an identical page (no cart/session data baked in) — if so, full-page caching at the CDN/edge is the bigger win since it skips your app servers entirely; if pages are personalized, cache at the data layer instead (Redis, keyed by product id, read-through on miss).

The fork that actually matters is invalidation: TTL-only is simpler but means stale prices/stock for up to the TTL window; event-driven invalidation (bust the key on write) is accurate but couples your write path to the cache. For product data, use both — invalidate on write, keep a short TTL (~1-5 min) as a backstop for anything that bypasses the write path.

Left out: cache stampede protection (locking/request coalescing on a popular product's miss) and warming strategy — worth designing once you pick the above.

The CDN is already in front of every request (CDN.md) and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends, but hit rate is 0% because `middleware/security.js` sends `no-store` on every route, including `/p` — that was the app-wide fix for a 2024 finding where an *account* page leaked between users via an intermediary cache. `/p` was swept in by accident: `routes/products.js` reads no session and nothing on it varies by user, so it's safe to cache; `/account` genuinely isn't and must keep `no-store`.

**Build it as:** split `security.js` into two policies — `/account` keeps the current `no-store, private`; `/p` gets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<N>, stale-while-revalidate=<M>`. That's it for delivery — no app-level cache layer, no Redis, because the CDN already sits there waiting and platform engineering won't add path rules, only respects origin headers.

The one real fork is **stock**. `productBySlug` (40ms) and `relatedProducts` (600ms, the four-table join that's your actual 900ms culprit) are pure catalog data, changing "a few times a day" — fine to cache for minutes. `stockFor` (250ms) is inventory, which moves continuously; baking it into a page cached for minutes risks showing sellable-but-actually-out items. Pick a TTL short enough that stale stock is tolerable (30-60s with stale-while-revalidate is standard for this) rather than splitting stock into a separate uncached fetch — that second path only earns its complexity if the business needs exact real-time counts on the page, which most storefronts don't (they show in-stock/low-stock buckets, not live numbers).

Depth left out: picking the actual TTL/SWR numbers against real catalog-edit and inventory-drift rates, and whether admin edits need a cache-purge hook instead of waiting out the TTL.

Reading the code: `app.js` clusters 4 worker processes per box with nothing shared in memory; `routes/api.js` resolves each request to a `client_id` via API key before any handler runs; `redis.js` is already the one thing every worker and every box has in common.

That fixes both forking decisions:

- **Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware already resolves it, and the comment above it says why IP is wrong here — clients hit from multiple addresses, and multiple clients share an address behind NAT.
- **Counter storage must be Redis, not in-process memory.** With 4 forked workers per box holding no shared state, an in-memory counter lets each worker grant the full limit independently — 4x the intended cap per box, worse across boxes.

Implementation: add a check as the first step after `req.client` is set in `routes/api.js:17` (before the DB queries in the route handlers), using an atomic Lua-scripted token bucket or `INCR`+`PEXPIRE` fixed window against `redis.js`'s client — atomic so concurrent requests from the same client don't race past the limit — returning `429` with `Retry-After` on rejection.

Left out: per-plan limits, which `req.client.plan` already gives you for free if you want tiered caps.

Rate-limit per client identity (API key/token, not IP — IP breaks for shared NATs/proxies and is trivial to rotate), using a token bucket counter in Redis (or your existing shared cache) keyed by client ID, enforced at the gateway/edge layer in front of `/v1` rather than in app code — that stops the hammering before it burns backend resources. Return `429` with a `Retry-After` header so well-behaved clients back off automatically.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Where the client identity comes from**: if `/v1` already requires auth, key on that token; if it's unauthenticated, you're stuck with IP/fingerprint heuristics, which is a materially weaker and gameable design.
- **Single instance vs fleet**: a single process can use an in-memory bucket; multiple instances need the counter in a shared store (Redis `INCR`+`EXPIRE`, or a sliding-window log) so limits are enforced fleet-wide instead of per-instance (which would let a client get N× the limit by round-robining).

Left out: burst allowances/tiered limits per plan, and alerting on repeat offenders — next level down once the basic gate is in place.

Recommend Server-Sent Events (SSE): the dashboard opens one persistent HTTP connection, the server pushes an event whenever the underlying data changes, and the browser just updates the DOM — no client polling, and SSE auto-reconnects on drop. Two decisions actually fork the design:

1. **Push vs. poll** — if changes are infrequent or near-real-time isn't critical, a 5-15s `setInterval` fetch is far less infrastructure for similar user-perceived freshness. SSE wins when updates are frequent or latency matters.
2. **Fan-out if you run multiple server instances** — a single process can just push directly, but with multiple app servers you need something to broadcast the change to whichever instance holds the client's connection (Redis pub/sub, Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, or a managed service like Pusher/Ably).

Which of those matches your setup — single server or several instances behind a load balancer?

Poll, not push — the platform forces this. `PLATFORM.md` says WebSocket upgrades 501 at the edge and functions are frozen/killed at 10s, which also rules out a long-lived SSE stream from `api/`. So there's no channel to push through; the only lever left is how the client polls.

The other fork is interval length, and `jobs/rollup.md` settles it too: `rollup` only changes once a minute, on the minute, written by a single scheduled job. Polling faster than that just reloads identical rows — `db.js` even calls that out. Poll every 15–20s and skip the re-render when `computed_at` hasn't changed from the last response.

Concretely: change `public/dashboard.js`'s `load()` (currently only wired to the click handler and the initial `window.load`) to also run on a `setInterval`, keep a `lastComputedAt` in closure, and only call `render(rows)` when the new `computed_at` differs. `api/metrics.js` needs no change — it's already a cheap, cacheless read (~30ms, 4KB).

Left out: backoff/pause when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilitychange`) and what happens if a poll fails — worth deciding but secondary to the interval choice above.

The core issue: a timeout is not a known failure — you don't know if the charge landed on the processor's side. Retrying blindly risks a double charge; showing "failed" when it actually succeeded loses the sale and confuses the customer. Design around that ambiguity, not around "retry the request":

1. **Idempotency key per attempt** — generate one before the first call (e.g. tied to order/invoice ID) and send it on every retry. This is the precondition for retrying at all; without it, a retry after a timeout can create a second charge.
2. **Classify the error before deciding to retry.** Timeouts, 5xx, and network errors are retryable; declines (insufficient funds, card rejected) are not — those should fail fast with a real reason, not get retried.
3. **Retry with backoff, bounded** (e.g. 3 attempts, exponential backoff), reusing the same idempotency key each time so the gateway dedupes.
4. **If still unresolved after retries, don't show "failed"** — persist the charge as `pending` and reconcile asynchronously: poll the gateway or wait on its webhook for the definitive status, then update the order. Show the customer "processing," not a false failure.
5. **State machine + reconciliation job** backing this: `pending → succeeded/failed`, with a background job sweeping anything stuck in `pending` past a threshold, so a lost webhook doesn't strand an order forever.

The fork that matters most: synchronous retry (a couple of quick attempts in the request path) vs. going straight to async pending+reconcile. Given timeouts a few times a day, I'd do a couple of quick synchronous retries first (cheap, fixes most cases immediately), then fall back to async reconciliation for whatever's still unresolved.

Root cause: on a timeout you don't actually know whether the charge went through on the processor's side, so a naive retry risks a double charge. The fix has to be built around that uncertainty, not just "try again."

**Recommendation:** generate an idempotency key per charge attempt (most processors — Stripe, Braintree, Adyen — support this natively) and reuse that exact key for every retry of the same logical charge. That makes retrying safe by construction: if the first attempt actually succeeded, the processor returns the original result instead of charging again. Then retry automatically a couple of times with short backoff before ever surfacing failure to the customer, and only show "payment failed" when the processor returns a real decline (card declined, insufficient funds) rather than a timeout/network error — those are different failure classes and should produce different UI copy.

The one fork worth deciding up front: **inline synchronous retry vs. async reconciliation.** Inline (retry within the same request, bounded to a second or two) is simpler and fine if timeouts are usually transient/fast. If timeouts can be long or frequent, move the retry to a background job — return "processing" to the customer, retry/poll the charge status with the same idempotency key, then notify (webhook/websocket/email) once resolved. That's a bigger architectural change (needs a pending-charge state and a way to update the customer asynchronously) so it's worth confirming which failure mode you're actually seeing before committing to it.

Left out: backoff/circuit-breaker tuning, and a periodic reconciliation sweep for charges left in a pending/unknown state (e.g., process crashed mid-retry) — that's the next layer down once the above is in place.

Recommend Postgres full-text search: add a `tsvector` column combining name + description, index it with GIN, query via `to_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` on the user's words. Update the vector via a trigger or on write so it stays in sync — no separate infra needed if you're already on Postgres.

Two things that fork this: catalog size and whether you need typo-tolerance/ranking-by-relevance-signals (popularity, stock). Small-to-medium catalog with exact/stemmed matching, Postgres is enough. Large catalog or fuzzy/faceted search, move to a dedicated engine (Typesense/OpenSearch/Algolia) fed by the same write path via CDC or an outbox.

What's your current database and rough catalog size — that decides which fork applies.

Recommend Postgres full-text search over a dedicated search engine, unless the catalog is large or typo-tolerance/faceting is a hard requirement.

- Add a generated `tsvector` column combining name + description (name weighted higher), GIN-indexed, updated automatically on insert/update.
- Search endpoint takes the query string, runs `plainto_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` against that column, ranks with `ts_rank`, returns top N.

The fork that actually matters: catalog size and tolerance for typos/fuzzy matches. Postgres FTS handles thousands to low millions of rows fine and needs zero new infrastructure; if you need instant-as-you-type results, typo correction, or synonym/faceted search at scale, that's the point to reach for Typesense/Meilisearch/OpenSearch instead — a separate indexing pipeline and infra decision, worth punting until the simpler approach proves insufficient.

Recommendation: presigned direct-to-storage upload, not proxied through your app server. Client requests a signed PUT URL (S3/GCS/R2) from the backend, uploads the file straight to the bucket, then tells the backend to attach that object key to the listing. Keeps large binaries off your app servers and scales for free.

Two decisions that actually fork this:

- **Compress client-side before upload.** Phone photos run 3–10MB and are often HEIC. Resize/re-encode to JPEG (~1600px long edge, ~85% quality) in the browser/app before the PUT — cuts upload time and storage cost, and sidesteps HEIC-decoding gaps in some backends/CDNs. Do EXIF orientation fix here too, or photos land sideways.
- **Process the rest async, not inline.** Thumbnail generation, further compression, and moderation/safety scanning happen in a background job after the object lands in the bucket (S3 event → queue → worker). The listing shows the photo as "processing" until that job finishes and swaps in the CDN URL. Don't block the upload response on this.

Depth left out: presigned-URL auth/expiry scheme, multi-photo ordering/reordering UI, and moderation-queue policy for flagged images.

Recommended shape: client resizes/re-encodes the photo (canvas downscale to ~2000px longest edge, fix EXIF orientation, convert HEIC to JPEG) before uploading, sends it straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2/Blob) via a presigned URL your server issues, then the server just records the reference and enqueues a background job to generate thumbnail/display variants — the listing shows a placeholder until that job confirms.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Direct-to-storage vs. proxied through your app server.** For phone-camera-size files (often 3–12MB), proxying doubles bandwidth and ties up a request thread; presigned direct upload is the right call unless you need to scan/transform before storage.
- **Client-side resize before upload vs. accept raw and resize server-side.** Client-side saves upload time and data on cellular and is worth it for a seller-facing mobile flow, at the cost of more JS and inconsistent output across browsers; server-side is simpler on the client but you pay full upload cost for unresized photos.

Left out: variant-size strategy, moderation/scanning, and resumable upload for flaky mobile connections — next-level details once storage backend is picked.

Cache-aside on the product read path: key by product id (plus locale/currency if those vary the query), store the assembled product data in Redis with a TTL, and invalidate that key when the product is edited rather than waiting out the TTL.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **What you cache** — the raw DB rows/query result vs. the fully rendered page fragment. Cache the query result if any part of the page is per-user (pricing, inventory, "in your cart"); cache the rendered HTML if the page is identical for every visitor, since that skips template rendering too.
2. **How it goes stale** — pure TTL (simple, but customers can see stale prices/stock for up to the TTL) vs. invalidate-on-write from wherever products get edited (fresher, but only works if all write paths go through one place you can hook).

Left out: cache stampede protection (many requests missing the same key at once and all hitting the DB together) and warming — worth designing once you pick the two above.

Cache-aside at the data layer: on a page load, look up the assembled product object (not raw rows) in Redis by product ID (+ locale/currency if those vary pricing), and on a miss run the DB query and populate the cache. Use a short TTL (minutes) as a backstop, plus explicit invalidation triggered by product/price/inventory writes, so stale data is bounded even if the invalidation path misses an edge case.

Two decisions actually fork this design:

1. **What layer to cache** — full rendered page/fragment (bigger win, ~900ms→cache-hit latency) vs. just the DB query result (safer, avoids re-cache-keying on every input that changes the page like session state or A/B flags). Given "nearly all of it is the DB," caching the query/object layer gets most of the win with less invalidation surface — start there before reaching for full-page caching.
2. **Invalidation strategy** — TTL-only is simplest but risks showing stale price/stock after an admin edit; event-driven invalidation (write path publishes a "product changed" event that purges the key) is correct but requires every write path to actually fire it, including bulk imports and admin tools.

Token bucket per client key (API key or auth token, not raw IP — one client behind a shared NAT shouldn't cost others), enforced at the edge (gateway/proxy) before requests reach `/v1`, returning 429 with a `Retry-After` header so the client backs off instead of retrying into the wall.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Where state lives**: a single-instance limiter (in-process counter) is fine if `/v1` runs on one box; behind multiple instances you need shared state (Redis `INCR`+`EXPIRE` or a token-bucket script) or clients can burst past the limit by hitting different instances.
- **Identifying the offender**: if this client doesn't authenticate before `/v1`, you can't key on client ID and you're stuck rate-limiting by IP/connection, which is weaker.

What's your `/v1` stack — is there already a gateway (nginx, Envoy, Kong) in front of it, or is this limiting to be added in the app itself?

Key the limit on `req.client.client_id`, not IP — the auth middleware in `routes/api.js` already resolves this, and its own comment notes IP is unreliable here (NAT sharing, multi-address clients).

Store the counter in Redis (`redis.js`), since it's already the only state shared across the 4 cluster workers per box and across boxes (`app.js`'s workers share nothing in module scope) — an in-memory counter would undercount by workers×boxes and let the same client through repeatedly.

Concretely: a fixed-window `INCR` + `PEXPIRE` on `ratelimit:{client_id}:{minute}` in Redis, checked in a new middleware placed right after the auth middleware (where `req.client` becomes available, before any Postgres work runs). Compare against a limit derived from `req.client.plan`; over it, return `429` with `Retry-After`.

Left for the next level down: fixed-window allows a 2x burst at window boundaries — swap in a Lua-scripted token bucket if that turns out to matter in practice.

Push data from server to client instead of the browser polling — for a read-only dashboard, use Server-Sent Events (SSE): the server holds a connection open and streams updates as they happen, the client just listens and re-renders.

The one real fork: SSE vs WebSockets vs short-interval polling.
- Polling (e.g. every 5-10s) is simplest to build and debug, but adds latency and load proportional to dashboard count.
- SSE is push, one-way, works over plain HTTP, auto-reconnects in the browser — right fit since a dashboard only receives, never sends.
- WebSockets are full-duplex, more moving parts (ping/pong, reconnect logic) — only worth it if the dashboard also needs to send commands back.

Second fork, orthogonal: what triggers the push. Either the backend emits an event whenever the underlying data changes (event-driven, needs a pub/sub like Redis/NATS if there's more than one server instance), or a lightweight poller inside the server diffs the data source on an interval and pushes only on change. Which one applies depends on whether the source data (DB, metrics store, etc.) can notify you directly — what's it backed by?

The real fork is push vs. poll:

- **Poll**: client re-fetches on an interval (e.g. every 5–15s). Simplest to build, works with any existing REST endpoint, but wastes requests when nothing changed and has a visible lag.
- **Push (SSE or WebSocket)**: server sends updates when data actually changes. For a dashboard that only needs server→client updates, **SSE** is the better fit — it's plain HTTP, auto-reconnects, and is much simpler than WebSockets, which you'd only need if the dashboard also sends data back up.

Recommendation: SSE endpoint that streams updates, with the backend emitting an event whenever the underlying metric/status changes (or on a cheap server-side interval if the source itself has to be polled). Client keeps a single `EventSource` open and patches the DOM/state on each message, falling back to a slow poll if the connection drops.

Left out: how the backend detects "changed" (DB triggers/pub-sub vs. server-side polling of the source), auth on a long-lived connection, and reconnection/backoff behavior — depends on your stack, which I don't have visibility into here (empty, non-git workspace).

Build it as: retry only transient failures, and make retries idempotent so a slow charge that actually went through doesn't get double-charged.

**Idempotency key** is the load-bearing piece — generate one per checkout attempt (not per HTTP request) and pass it to the payment provider on every retry of that attempt. A timeout doesn't tell you whether the charge landed; without an idempotency key, retrying blind risks a double charge, and skipping the retry risks losing a payment that actually succeeded.

**Classify the failure before deciding to retry.** Timeouts, network errors, and 5xx/rate-limit responses are retryable; declines, insufficient funds, and invalid-card responses are not — retrying those just delays the same "payment failed" message and can trip the provider's fraud checks.

**Where the retry loop lives** is the other fork: inline (block the request a few seconds and retry synchronously) versus async (return "processing" immediately, retry via background job/queue, and notify the customer through webhook/polling/email on resolution). Given charges are timing out "a few times a day," inline retries risk stacking a second slow request on top of a slow provider; async with backoff (e.g., a queued job retrying at 2s/10s/30s, capped at 3-5 attempts) is the more robust default and also fixes the UX complaint — the customer sees "processing" instead of a false "failed."

Left out: what to show the customer while a retry is in flight, and how far to back off / cap total wait before surfacing a real failure — those are the next-level details once the sync-vs-async call is made.

The core issue: a timeout means "unknown", not "failed" — the charge may have gone through on the gateway's side even though your request didn't get a response. Retrying blindly risks double-charging; showing "failed" when it might have succeeded risks losing the sale or confusing the customer.

Design:
- **Idempotency key per charge attempt**, generated client- or server-side once per checkout, sent on every retry of that same attempt. Stripe/most gateways dedupe on this key, so retrying is safe even if the original request actually landed.
- **Classify the error before deciding what to show.** A timeout/network error is retryable and ambiguous; a decline (insufficient funds, fraud block) is terminal and should show "failed" immediately — don't lump them together as you're doing now.
- On timeout, don't surface "failed" — mark the payment as `processing`, retry the same idempotent request a couple of times with short backoff, and if still unresolved, resolve it out-of-band (poll the gateway for the charge status by idempotency key, or wait for its webhook) rather than blocking the customer's request.

The one real fork: resolve the ambiguous case **synchronously** (retry inline, customer waits a few extra seconds for a definite answer) vs **asynchronously** (show "processing", confirm via webhook/poll and update after). Given it's only a few times a day, async is simpler and avoids holding the request open — pick that unless checkout UX requires an immediate yes/no.

Left out: backoff/attempt-limit tuning and the reconciliation job's polling schedule — second-order once the idempotency key and async path are in place.

Postgres full-text search on the existing table, not a separate search service — at ~38K rows and low growth, `products` fits entirely in a GIN index with room to spare, and pulling in Elasticsearch/Algolia would just add an infra dependency and a sync problem for no benefit at this scale.

Concretely: add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weight A) and `description` (weight B) via `setweight`, put a GIN index on it, and add `GET /products/search?q=` in `routes/products.js` that runs `websearch_to_tsquery` against it, ordered by `ts_rank`. `db.js`'s plain `pool.query` needs no changes.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Weighting** — giving `name` more weight than `description` (via `setweight('A')`/`setweight('B')`) is what makes a name match outrank a description match; skipping this and treating both fields equally will make results feel wrong even though search "works."
- **Generated column + GIN vs. `ILIKE` on the fly** — `ILIKE '%term%'` needs no schema change but can't rank relevance and gets slow as `OR`s stack up; the tsvector approach costs a migration but gives you ranking and stays fast as the catalog grows.

38K products in Postgres already — that's well within Postgres full-text search range, so no new infra: add a generated `tsvector` column over `name`/`description` with a GIN index, and query it with `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word "a few words" input naturally) ranked by `ts_rank`.

The one real fork is typo tolerance. Plain `tsvector` does stemming but not fuzzy matching, so "sheker" won't find "sneaker." If that matters, add `pg_trgm` on `name` and blend a trigram similarity fallback/boost — still just Postgres, no new service. If it doesn't, skip it and ship the simpler tsvector-only version.

I'd start tsvector-only, since it's a small addition to `schema.sql` and a new `GET /products?q=` handler alongside the existing route — and add trigram only if users actually complain about typos.

Direct-to-storage upload: client gets a short-lived presigned URL from your API, uploads straight to S3/GCS, then calls the API to attach the resulting key to the listing. Server never touches the image bytes, which matters once sellers are sending multiple phone-camera photos over cellular. A storage-triggered function then generates thumbnails/variants and flips the photo to "ready."

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Compress on-device first** (resize to ~1600px, HEIC→JPEG) rather than uploading raw camera output — phone photos run 5–15MB each, and doing this client-side cuts upload time and data usage a lot. Skip it only if you need untouched originals.
- **Attach-after-upload, not attach-during-draft** — the client uploads to storage, then explicitly tells your API "this key belongs to listing X." That way a dropped connection mid-upload leaves an orphaned storage object instead of a half-broken listing record.

Left out: resumable-upload/retry mechanics, content moderation scanning, CDN delivery, and cleanup of orphaned uploads — each is a follow-up if you want to go deeper.

Signed PUT direct-to-S3 — the path `storage.js` already half-built (`signedUrl` supports `method: 'PUT'`, bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`, nothing calls it yet).

Why: nginx's `client_max_body_size` is `1m` globally, and per-location overrides were explicitly declined because the limit is cited in the payments team's PCI paperwork. A phone camera photo is routinely several MB, so routing the bytes through the storefront listener isn't an option — they have to go around nginx entirely.

Flow:
1. Client asks the storefront for a signed PUT URL for a new key (a small JSON call, well under 1m).
2. Client PUTs the photo bytes straight to S3, never touching nginx.
3. Client confirms completion back to the storefront, which calls `db.addPhotoKey` to append the key to `listings.photo_keys`.
4. Reads reuse the existing per-key signed-GET pattern already used for invoices.

Two things that fork this:
- Validation (listing ownership, content-type/size limits) has to happen at step 1, before the PUT URL is issued — the server never sees the bytes to check them.
- Step 3 is required, not optional: S3 doesn't call back on upload, so without a confirm step a client that dies mid-flow leaves an orphaned S3 object and no key in Postgres.

Left out: thumbnailing/moderation, multi-photo ordering, retry/resume — next level down.

Two separate problems here, both visible in the files.

**The CDN cache is being defeated app-wide.** `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` on every response, applied globally after a 2024 audit finding about `/account` leaking cross-user data through an intermediary cache. `/p` got swept in "because that was the fastest way to close the finding," not because it needed it — `routes/products.js` says the page is anonymous, reads no session, and is identical for everyone. The CDN already sits in front of every request and honors origin headers with no path rules (`CDN.md`), so fixing the header on `/p` alone would let the CDN absorb most traffic before it ever reaches the app — that's the biggest win available and it's free.

**Split the middleware**, don't touch `/account`: give `/p` a real `Cache-Control` (e.g. `public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300`) while `/account` keeps the current `no-store, private`. That's the one fork that matters here — the header is a blanket app-wide default standing in for a per-route decision, and un-blanketing it is what the audit and last quarter's "policy belongs in the app" ruling both point toward.

For the requests that still hit origin (cache misses, revalidation), `db.js` shows the 900ms isn't uniform: `relatedProducts` (~600ms, four-table join) and `stockFor` (~250ms) are the cost, and they have different volatility — catalog edits happen a few times a day, inventory moves faster. Don't cache them together at one TTL. Cache `relatedProducts` on product id with a TTL measured in minutes-to-hours since it barely changes; keep `stockFor` on a much shorter TTL (seconds) or leave it out of the cached fragment entirely, since stale stock is the kind of staleness that actually costs money (overselling), unlike a stale "related items" list.

Recommendation: put a read-through cache (Redis) in front of the DB, keyed by product ID, with the query results (or rendered fragment) cached and a short TTL plus explicit invalidation on writes to that product.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Staleness tolerance** — if slightly stale data is fine, TTL-only (e.g. 60s) is simplest and needs no invalidation plumbing; if edits must show up immediately, you need cache invalidation wired into the product-update path, which is more moving parts.
- **What you cache** — caching the raw query result is simpler and composes with other logic, but caching the fully rendered page/fragment cuts more latency since you skip rendering too.

Depth I'm skipping: cache stampede protection (locking/early refresh) and multi-instance invalidation (pub/sub) — matter once you're past a single cache node or high concurrency.

Hook it into `routes/api.js` as middleware right after the key-auth block (routes/api.js:9-19) — that's where `req.client.client_id` and `.plan` already get resolved, and it's the one place every `/v1` request passes through regardless of worker. Key the limit on `client_id`, not IP: the auth middleware's own comment notes clients share NAT'd addresses and use multiple ones, so IP-based limiting would throttle innocent neighbors and miss the actual offender.

For storage, reuse `redis.js` — it's already the one piece of state shared across all 4 workers × N boxes (per app.js:3-6), so it's the only place a global counter can live; per-worker in-memory counting would let a client get 4x (or more) the intended rate depending on which process handles each request.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Algorithm**: fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` is cheap but allows a 2x burst across a window boundary — since the problem is exactly bursty hammering, a token-bucket (Lua script doing atomic check-and-decrement) holds up better.
- **Limit tier**: `req.client.plan` is already on hand, so quotas should be per-plan, not a single global number — otherwise you're either too strict for high-tier clients or too loose to protect anyone from a low-tier abuser.

Respond 429 with `Retry-After` on rejection. The Lua script itself (atomic get-timestamp/refill/decrement) is the next level of detail if you want to go there.

Two decisions actually fork this design; everything else is detail.

**Key by `client_id`, not IP.** The auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19` already resolves the API key to `req.client.client_id` before your two routes run — and the comment there notes clients share NAT'd IPs with others. IP-based limiting would throttle innocent clients sharing an address with the offender, or fail to catch a client rotating IPs. Rate limit after auth, on `client_id` (and pull `plan` from that same row to set per-tier limits — no extra query needed).

**State goes in Redis, not process memory.** `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with nothing shared between them, and `redis.js` already gives you one Redis shared across every worker on every box — the same reason sessions live there. An in-memory counter per worker would let a client get 4x (or Nx-boxes-x) the intended limit by landing on different workers.

Concretely: middleware in `routes/api.js` right after the auth block, running a small Lua script against `redis.js`'s client that does an atomic increment-and-check on key `rl:{client_id}:{window}` with a TTL, returning 429 + `Retry-After` on overflow. Lua (or `MULTI`) matters because plain `INCR` then `EXPIRE` as two round-trips races under concurrent requests from the same client.

Left out: fixed-window vs. sliding-window-counter vs. token-bucket precision trade-off, and the actual per-plan numbers — pick those once you know how bursty legitimate traffic is.

Push, not poll: have the backend emit updates over Server-Sent Events (a single `/events` endpoint the dashboard subscribes to), and have the frontend patch just the changed widgets instead of refetching everything. That avoids the thundering-herd problem you get from every client polling on a timer, and SSE is simpler to operate than WebSockets when updates only flow server→client.

Two decisions actually fork the design:
- **Push vs. poll** — if the data only changes every few minutes and staleness of a minute is fine, plain polling (`setInterval` fetch, maybe with `visibilitychange` to pause when the tab's backgrounded) is less infrastructure than SSE/WebSockets and may just be the better call.
- **Where "changed" is computed** — either the backend diffs and pushes only deltas, or it pushes full snapshots and the client diffs for rendering. Deltas scale better with many widgets; snapshots are simpler to reason about and debug.

Everything else (reconnect/backoff, an initial full fetch on connect, a "data as of" timestamp in the UI) is standard plumbing once those two are picked. What's the current dashboard built on — is there already a backend that could hold open connections, or is it static/serverless?

Recommendation: server-sent events (SSE) — the backend pushes updates over a long-lived HTTP connection, the dashboard just renders what arrives. Simpler than WebSockets (no bidirectional handshake, auto-reconnects natively) and dashboards only need server-to-client updates.

Two decisions that actually fork the design:

1. **Push vs. poll.** If update latency can tolerate a few seconds, skip the infra work entirely: poll on an interval (e.g. `refetchInterval` in react-query/SWR) and let ETags/conditional requests keep it cheap. Only go to SSE/WebSockets if you need near-real-time or the polling load becomes a problem at your traffic.
2. **What triggers a push.** Either the backend re-runs the dashboard's query on a timer and diffs/broadcasts changes, or it reacts to the actual write path (DB trigger, outbox, CDC stream) and pushes immediately. The former is much less plumbing; the latter is the only way to get true "instant" updates.

Given it's an internal ops dashboard, I'd start with polling-with-a-reasonable-interval, and only move to SSE if staleness becomes a real complaint. Left out: auth/reconnect handling for SSE, backpressure if many clients, and how you'd diff/batch updates server-side — next level down once you pick a direction.

Two things are broken here, not one: there's no idempotency key, and `checkout.js` treats "timeout" the same as "declined" (payments.js:5-6, PROVIDER.md's own guidance says a timeout is *unknown*, never failed).

**Approach:** Generate an idempotency key per pay attempt (e.g. `order.id` + a stored attempt id), send it as `Idempotency-Key` on every call to Cardstream. That makes it safe to retry a timed-out charge — Cardstream returns the original charge instead of authorizing twice. Put the retry loop inside `payments.charge()`: on `timeout`/connection error, retry with backoff (a few bounded attempts, since this is in the request path and the customer is waiting; rate limit is a non-issue at 600/min). Don't retry on a 4xx decline — that's a real failure, not an unknown.

**The fork that matters:** what happens if retries are still inconclusive after the last attempt. Don't let that fall through to `res.status(502).json({ error: "payment failed" })` like it does now (checkout.js:29) — that's telling the customer a charge failed when Cardstream says it might have gone through. Set the order to a `pending`/`processing` status instead, return that to the customer, and resolve it out-of-band (a reconciliation job that looks up the charge by idempotency key, or a webhook if Cardstream has one) rather than guessing.

Left out: backoff tuning, how the idempotency key is persisted across retries within one request vs. across separate user-initiated retries, and the reconciliation job's own design.

Based on `payments.js` and `PROVIDER.md`: a timeout here is explicitly *unknown*, not failed — the vendor may have authorized before the connection died. The route's `catch` currently collapses that into the same "payment failed" as a real decline, which is the actual bug.

The build:

1. **Idempotency key per order, not per request.** Add an `idempotency_key` column on `orders`, generate it once (e.g. when the order enters checkout), and send it as the `Idempotency-Key` header on every charge call for that order, including retries. That's what makes retrying safe — the vendor dedupes and returns the same charge id instead of double-authorizing.

2. **Retry only on timeout/network error, never on a 4xx decline**, with the same key, a couple of bounded attempts and backoff (well under the 600/min limit, so no rate-limit concern).

3. **If it's still unknown after retries, don't answer "failed."** Set order status to something like `processing` (not `pending` — the handler's `order.status !== "pending"` guard would otherwise let a second checkout POST slip through with the same order in a still-ambiguous state) and reconcile out of band: a background job that re-sends the charge with the stored key until it gets a definitive result, or a vendor webhook if Cardstream offers one. The customer sees "processing," not a wrong terminal state.

The two decisions that actually fork the design: where the key is generated and persisted (per-order in the DB, so it survives retries and process restarts — not per-HTTP-request), and what happens when retries are exhausted (report `processing` and reconcile async, rather than ever reporting `failed` for something that was only ever a timeout). Everything below that — exact backoff curve, whether reconciliation is a cron job or a queue — is implementation detail.

Given the scale here — 38k products, Postgres 16 already — this doesn't need a separate search engine; Postgres full-text search covers it:

Add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, with a GIN index, then query with `to_tsquery`/`websearch_to_tsquery` ranked by `ts_rank`. New endpoint in `routes/products.js` alongside the existing list route, same `db.query` pool.

The one real fork: Postgres FTS vs. an external engine (Elasticsearch/Algolia/Meilisearch). At this row count and growth rate, FTS wins — no new infra, no sync pipeline, sub-10ms queries with the GIN index. Only reconsider that if you outgrow single-node Postgres or need typo-tolerance/faceting beyond what `pg_trgm` gives you.

Left out: ranking/relevance tuning, and whether "a few words" should also fuzzy-match typos (`pg_trgm` similarity is the usual bolt-on if so).

Two things fork this before anything else:

**Scale/relevance needs.** For a catalog up to ~100k products, Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` column + GIN index, or `pg_trgm` for typo-tolerant substring matching) gets you there with no new infra — index name+description, rank with `ts_rank`. Past that, or if you need typo tolerance, faceting, or synonym handling, a dedicated engine (Typesense, Meilisearch, or Elasticsearch) is the better call — worth it once search quality itself becomes a product concern, not before.

**Freshness vs simplicity.** A search index needs to stay in sync with product edits — either reindex on write (simple, fine at low write volume) or via a queue/CDC pipeline (needed once writes are frequent enough that synchronous reindexing adds latency to product updates).

Recommendation: start with Postgres `tsvector` + GIN, reindex synchronously on product save. Migrate to a dedicated search engine only when you hit its ceiling (relevance complaints, catalog size, or need for typo tolerance).

Presigned-URL upload straight to object storage (S3/GCS), not proxied through your app server — phone photos run 5-15MB each and multiple per listing, so routing them through your API just to relay to storage wastes server bandwidth/memory for no benefit.

The fork that matters: resize/compress client-side before upload, or accept the raw file and process after.

- Client-side (canvas/File API resize to ~2000px longest edge, JPEG re-encode) cuts upload time and storage cost, but adds complexity — HEIC from iPhones doesn't decode in `<canvas>` in Safari, so you still need a fallback.
- Upload raw, process server-side via a background job (thumbnail, EXIF orientation fix, strip GPS metadata) is simpler on the client and handles HEIC uniformly, at the cost of a slower perceived upload on cell connections.

I'd default to raw upload + async server-side processing unless upload latency on cellular is a measured complaint — it's less client code to get wrong across iOS/Android/mobile-web.

Left out: listing-to-photo data model and ordering, upload progress/retry UX, and moderation/content-scanning pipeline — next-level details once the transport approach is picked.

Direct-to-S3 presigned PUT, reusing what's already half-built: `storage.signedUrl(key, {method: 'PUT'})` is wired up and unused, and the bucket CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`. The app server never touches the bytes.

Flow: client calls the API for a signed PUT URL (issues a key like `listings/{id}/{uuid}.jpg`, doesn't touch `photo_keys` yet), the browser/app PUTs the file straight to S3, then calls back to the API with the key to run `db.addPhotoKey`.

This isn't really optional — it's forced by `nginx.conf`: `client_max_body_size 1m` is global on that listener and was explicitly declined for PCI reasons, with per-location overrides also declined. A phone photo routinely runs 3–12MB, so any path that proxies bytes through `storefront:3000` is a dead end before it starts.

The one real fork: `getSignedUrl` + `PutObjectCommand` (what `storage.js` already has) gives you a bare presigned PUT with no size/content-type enforcement — S3 will accept whatever bytes hit that URL. `createPresignedPost` instead gives you policy conditions (`content-length-range`, `content-type`) enforced by S3 itself, at the cost of a different client upload shape (multipart form, not a raw PUT) and a helper that doesn't exist yet. Given there's no size cap anywhere else in this path once you're off the nginx listener, I'd add the POST-policy version rather than extend the PUT one.

Left out: confirming the object landed before trusting the key (a client that PUTs then never calls back leaves nothing in `photo_keys`, which is safe, but a client that calls back with a key it never uploaded needs a HeadObject check or you get broken image links), EXIF/orientation stripping, thumbnailing for the listing grid, and cleanup of orphaned S3 objects from abandoned uploads.

Read-through cache in front of the DB, keyed by product id, populated on miss and invalidated on write — that's the standard shape for a page that's read-heavy and DB-bound.

Two decisions actually fork this:

- **What you cache**: raw query results (flexible, but still pays render cost) vs. the fully rendered page/fragment (fastest, but you invalidate more surface area on any content or template change). For a product page, caching the assembled page data (post-query, pre-render or post-render) usually wins since the queries are the 900ms, not the rendering.
- **Invalidation**: TTL-only (simple, but stale price/stock windows) vs. event-driven bust on product update (accurate, but requires every write path to know to invalidate). Given products change on writes you control, bust-on-write plus a longer TTL safety net is the usual pick over TTL-only.

Left out at this depth: cache store choice (Redis vs in-process), stampede protection on cold keys, and cache-key versioning for schema changes — next level down once the two above are settled.

**Root cause of the 0% hit rate:** `middleware/security.js` sets `no-store` app-wide (app.js:9) because of a 2024 audit finding about `/account` leaking between users. It was applied to `/p` too, "the fastest way to close the finding," and never revisited — even though the product page (routes/products.js:6-8) is anonymous and identical for every user. The CDN (CDN.md) already sits in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends, so the fix is edge caching via headers, not a new cache layer.

**Change:** stop sending `no-store` on `/p`. Either scope `security.js`'s cache headers to `/account` only, or have the product route set its own `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` after the middleware runs, overriding it. Leave `/account` exactly as-is — that route is the one the audit finding was actually about, and `db.ordersForUser` is genuinely per-user. On a cache hit the CDN serves the response and the 900ms DB path (dominated by the 600ms `relatedProducts` join) never runs.

**The one real fork — stock:** `productBySlug` and `relatedProducts` only change on admin edits ("a few times a day"), so a multi-minute TTL is safe. `stockFor` changes on every order, so caching it at the same TTL as the rest of the page risks showing stale stock. Simplest option: cache the whole rendered page at a short TTL (~30-60s) and accept brief stock staleness — fine for a "few left" indicator. Alternative: split stock into its own low-TTL/no-store fragment, cache product+related separately at a longer TTL. Start with the simple whole-page TTL; it's a one-line change and captures nearly all the win. Left out: purge-on-admin-edit, so a product update shows up immediately instead of waiting out the TTL — worth doing, but a layer on top, not required to fix the 900ms.

Since `req.client.client_id` is already resolved by the auth middleware in `routes/api.js:9-19`, and `redis.js` already gives every worker/box a shared store, that's where the limiter goes: a new middleware right after the key lookup, keyed by `client_id` (not IP — the comment on `api.js:6-8` says one client uses many IPs and several clients share a NAT'd IP, so IP-keying would both under- and over-block). Track it in Redis with `INCR sess:... ` style keys (e.g. `rl:{client_id}:{windowStart}`) and `PEXPIRE` set on first increment, so counting stays atomic across all four workers on every box without adding new infrastructure. Use the existing `plan` column to pick the limit per tier. On exceeding it, return 429 with `Retry-After` before the request touches `db.js`, since the actual damage is Postgres connection-pool exhaustion, not the Express layer itself.

The one real fork: fixed-window `INCR`+`EXPIRE` (two round trips, simple, slight burst at window edges) vs. a sliding-window/token-bucket Lua script (one round trip, smooth, more code). Given Redis is already a hard dependency here, I'd start with fixed-window and only move to a Lua-scripted token bucket if edge-of-window bursts turn out to matter. Left out: what to do for unauthenticated/pre-auth requests (they hit `db.query` for the key lookup itself before any limiter runs, so that path may need its own IP-based cap).

Key by `client_id`, not IP — the comment in `routes/api.js:6-8` notes clients share NAT addresses and use multiple ones, so IP limiting would both underlimit the abusive client and punish innocent neighbors. `client_id`/`plan` are already resolved in that auth middleware, so a rate check slots in right after it, before the DB queries in `/reports`.

Counter storage has to be Redis, not in-process. `app.js` forks 4 workers per box with no shared module state, and `redis.js` already documents Redis as "the only piece of state the workers have in common" — an in-memory counter would let each worker (and each box) grant the client its own separate quota. Use a fixed-window or sliding-window counter per `client_id` in Redis (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`, or a Lua script for atomicity), return `429` with `Retry-After` when the plan's limit is exceeded, and reject before the Postgres round-trip so an abusive client doesn't also monopolize DB connections.

Left out: exact limits per plan tier, burst vs sustained-rate tradeoffs (token bucket vs fixed window), and whether to rate-limit writes (`POST /reports`) more aggressively than reads.

Push data to the client instead of waiting for a request: SSE (or WebSocket if the dashboard ever needs to send data back) from the browser to a small endpoint that streams updates, replacing the polling/refresh loop.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Where updates originate** — event-driven (the write path that changes the underlying data publishes to a pub/sub channel like Redis/NATS, and the stream endpoint just relays) vs. timer-driven (server recomputes the dashboard query every N seconds and pushes if it changed). Event-driven is near-instant and cheaper at idle; timer-driven is far simpler if the data already comes from periodic batch jobs.
- **Transport** — SSE if updates only flow server-to-client (true for most dashboards, and it rides plain HTTP so it survives proxies/load balancers with no special config) vs. WebSocket if you need client-to-server too (filters, acks) or very high update frequency.

Left out: auth/reconnect handling on the stream, fanout scaling if there are many concurrent viewers, and whether to diff-and-patch the UI or just re-render on each push.

Depends on your stack, which I don't have here (empty workspace, no repo). Two things fork the design:

1. **Push vs. poll.** If the data changes are rare/bursty, use a push channel (SSE or WebSocket) instead of the dashboard polling an endpoint — SSE is the simpler choice for one-way "server tells client something changed" updates since it's plain HTTP with built-in reconnect, no need for WebSocket's bidirectional complexity.
2. **Where the change signal comes from.** Either the backend already has an event source (message queue, DB change stream, existing pub/sub) you can tap to emit SSE events, or it doesn't and you'd have the server poll its own data store on an interval and diff/broadcast — much cheaper to build but adds latency and DB load proportional to poll frequency.

Recommendation: SSE endpoint that streams updates, backed by whatever event source already exists in the backend; frontend keeps one connection open and patches state on each message.

What's the current dashboard built on (frontend framework, backend language, any existing queue/event bus)? That decides whether option 2 is "wire into what's there" or "add polling."

The core fix is distinguishing "timed out" from "failed" — a timeout means the charge's outcome is unknown, not negative, so blind retry risks a double charge.

Approach: on timeout, first re-query the processor for that charge's actual status using the original idempotency key, rather than immediately retrying. If it's still unresolved, retry the same request with that same idempotency key (so the processor collapses duplicates) via a background job with backoff, not inline in the original request. Only retry timeout/network/5xx errors — a real decline is terminal and shouldn't retry. Surface "processing" to the customer instead of "payment failed" until retries exhaust or resolve.

Two decisions actually fork this: idempotency key strategy (client-generated per checkout attempt vs. server-generated at charge time), and where the retry loop lives (synchronous before responding vs. async job reconciled by webhook). Which payment processor and stack is this on — that determines which of those is even available.

Core fix: make the charge idempotent, then retry automatically before the user ever sees "failed."

- Generate one idempotency key per logical charge attempt (order ID + amount, not per HTTP call) and send it on every retry. Stripe, Adyen, Braintree, etc. all support this — a retried request with the same key returns the original result instead of charging twice, which is the real risk once you retry on timeout.
- On timeout, don't assume failure — the charge may have gone through and only the response was lost. Before retrying, either replay with the same idempotency key (processor handles the dedup) or query the processor for that key's status. Only retry the ones that are genuinely ambiguous (timeout/network error), never a hard decline — that's a real failure and retrying won't change it.
- Persist charge state (`pending → succeeded/failed/timed_out`) so an attempt surviving a process crash mid-retry doesn't get resubmitted from scratch or lost.

The fork that actually matters: retry inline within the request (2-3 attempts, short backoff, user waits a couple extra seconds) vs. kick it to a background job/queue and update the order asynchronously once resolved (user sees "processing," not "failed"). Inline is simpler and fine if your timeouts are sub-second-to-a-few-seconds; async is the right call if the timeouts you're seeing are long enough that blocking the request would itself feel broken.

Left out: webhook reconciliation for charges that resolve after you've given up retrying, and how many attempts/backoff schedule to use — that's a number worth tuning against your actual timeout rate rather than guessing.

Two forking decisions:

**Index choice.** If products already live in Postgres and the catalog is small-to-mid size (tens of thousands of rows), Postgres full-text search (`tsvector` over name+description, GIN index) is enough and avoids a new service. If you need typo tolerance, faceting, or the catalog is large/high-QPS, use a dedicated engine (Meilisearch or Typesense are simplest to run; Elasticsearch if you already operate it) — worth it once "search" needs to feel instant and forgiving, not just match substrings.

**Freshness.** Sync the index on product write (in the same transaction/request) for simplicity, or via an async pipeline (CDC/outbox) if writes are high-volume and a few seconds of staleness is fine. Start synchronous; move to async only if write latency becomes a problem.

Recommendation: Postgres FTS to start — it's zero new infra and matches "type a few words, get matches by name/description" exactly. Migrate to Meilisearch/Typesense later if you need fuzzy matching or the catalog outgrows it.

Left out: relevance tuning (weighting name over description), autocomplete-as-you-type, synonyms, and filters/facets — those are the next layer once basic search is live.

For a catalog search like this, the fork is catalog size/growth, not tech novelty: under a few hundred thousand products, Postgres full-text search (a `tsvector` generated column combining name + description, GIN-indexed, ranked with `ts_rank`) gets you relevant multi-word matching with no new infrastructure; add `pg_trgm` alongside it if you need typo tolerance on partial words. Past that scale, or once you need faceting/synonyms/relevance tuning beyond what Postgres offers, move to a dedicated engine (Typesense/Meilisearch for simplicity, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for more control) — but that's a real infra addition, so I'd only reach for it once Postgres search actually falls short, not upfront.

What's the current data store — Postgres, something else?

Direct-to-storage upload with client-side compression first.

- **Client uploads straight to object storage (S3/GCS) via a presigned URL**, not proxied through your API server. Proxying lets you validate synchronously, but it means your server holds a stream open for the full mobile upload — slow and timeout-prone on cellular, and it doubles your bandwidth bill. Pick presigned URLs: your API just issues a short-lived signed PUT, the client uploads directly, then a storage "object created" event (or a client confirm call) triggers a background job to generate thumbnails/variants and attach the photo to the listing.
- **Downscale/re-encode on the client before uploading** (e.g. cap to ~2000px longest edge, JPEG). Phone camera originals run 3–15MB and are often HEIC; uploading them raw wastes the seller's data and slows the flow. Do it client-side for the win on upload time, but treat it as a courtesy, not the source of truth — re-encode/generate thumbnail sizes server-side too, since you can't trust every device/browser to compress correctly (or the request may come from an API client that skips it).

Left out: resumable/chunked upload for flaky connections, EXIF orientation handling, malware/content scanning, multi-photo ordering UI, and cleanup of orphaned uploads that never got attached to a listing.

The pieces here already point at one design, not several to weigh.

**The fork that matters: don't route photo bytes through the app server at all.** `nginx.conf` caps `client_max_body_size` at 1m globally, on purpose — it's shared with the payments listener and the payments team declined a per-location override for PCI reasons. A phone camera photo (2-12MB typically) would blow past that if it went through `proxy_pass http://storefront:3000`. Client-side compression to squeeze under 1MB is exactly the kind of fragile workaround that constraint is there to avoid.

`storage.js` already anticipated this: `signedUrl` supports `method: 'PUT'`, the bucket's CORS already allows PUT from `market.example.com`, and the comment says nothing uses it yet. That's the intended path — upload straight from the browser to S3, never touching nginx's body-size limit.

So the shape is:
1. `POST /listings/:id/photos/sign` — server calls `storage.signedUrl(key, { method: 'PUT' })` for a generated key (e.g. `listings/${id}/${uuid}.jpg`), returns the URL.
2. Browser PUTs the file bytes directly to S3 with that URL.
3. `POST /listings/:id/photos/confirm` — server calls `db.addPhotoKey(id, key)`, the same append-to-array helper that already exists and is currently unused.

`listings.photo_keys` is already a `text[]` sitting empty for this — no schema change needed, just the two small routes.

The other fork, sizing: compress client-side before the PUT anyway (canvas resize to ~1600px longest edge, JPEG ~80%), not for the nginx limit but because phone uploads are still real bytes over a real mobile connection — that's a UX/cost call, not a hard constraint like the nginx one.

The CDN already sits in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends — it's just that `middleware/security.js` (app.js:9) applies `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` globally, including to `/p`. That middleware was a blanket fix for an account-page leak; `/p` is anonymous, identical for every visitor, and changes only when someone edits the catalog. So the fix isn't "add caching," it's giving `/p` its own headers so the CDN you already pay for can do the work — that alone should take the 0% hit rate to near-100% for this route without touching `db.js`.
